atlas-th.0054: Employers that run formal programmes recruit at universities they know (SCB names only “leading Thai universities”), but the hiring criteria in the JobsDB report are the interview, work attitude and field of study, not the school.
atlas-th.0055: Co-operative education is common: Walailak places all its students for eight months, and SCB runs a four-month co-op. Both are placements arranged within a university programme.
atlas-th.0056: The Office of the Civil Service Commission’s 2026 general-knowledge exam (Part A) offered 450,000 paper seats at 14 test centres, with registration from 14 January to 3 February 2026, for people who had finished or would finish a diploma, bachelor’s or master’s in the 2026 academic year. No figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hiring was found.
atlas-th.0057: A company must have THB 2 million of paid-up capital and four Thai employees for each foreign employee it sponsors, unless it is promoted by the Board of Investment. See Visas for the rules.
atlas-th.0058: The sources disagree: a Thai-language CV guide lists the photo as not necessary unless the employer asks for it, while a CV-builder guide calls a 3 by 4 cm headshot at the top right common and often expected. Include one when the advert asks, and use the same format.
atlas-th.0059: A new graduate should keep the CV to one page; 1 to 2 pages is the range for 3 to 10 years of experience and up to 3 pages for executives. Give your name in Thai and English, and state your language levels.
atlas-th.0060: No source read states whether a cover letter is expected. On the portals you apply with the profile and CV; write a letter when a programme asks for it or when you apply directly to a person. This is our reading.
atlas-th.0061: Some employers check the past-employment references an applicant provides, and Thai law does not distinguish between checks before and after an offer; credential checks are standard practice at some firms.
atlas-th.0062: A foreign graduate who needs a work permit must supply a signed copy of the degree, and until 28 February 2027 the degree needs translation and consular legalisation.
atlas-th.0063: No source read states whether the application asks for an expected salary. JobThai offers salary-band searches (for example 100K and over), so have a figure in mind before you apply. This is our reading.
atlas-th.0064: Background checks vary widely by employer and role. Education and licence checks are standard at some firms, criminal-record checks (through the Royal Thai Police, with your consent) are often skipped unless the role handles money or children.
atlas-th.0065: Portals and programme pages take applications, and recruiters search uploaded résumé profiles; no survey of how much hiring runs through personal introductions was found, so this verdict is a judgement.
atlas-th.0066: Work needs a Non-Immigrant B visa and a work permit that the employer files after you arrive, and the employer must meet capital and Thai-staff rules, so an offer is hard to land from abroad without a sponsor.
atlas-th.0067: In the 2026 TOEIC survey 97% of Thai HR executives called English important and 80% used English assessments in recruitment; a CV-builder guide says Thai is the primary CV language, with an English version recommended for multinationals.
atlas-th.0068: Central Group’s Management Associate Program has seven stages: application, online test, first interview, open house, assessment centre, final interview and onboarding.
atlas-th.0069: English is tested: 80% of Thai HR executives in the ETS survey use English assessments in recruitment and screening, so expect a test or part of the interview in English.
atlas-th.0070: No source read gives the time from application to offer or a dress code; Personnel Consultant advises researching the company and the role before an interview and being ready to discuss your experience, strengths, goals and motivation.
atlas-th.0071: Probation typically lasts up to 119 days, because from 120 days an employee dismissed without cause is owed severance (30 days’ wages for 120 days to under 1 year, 90 days for 1 to under 3 years).
atlas-th.0072: Notice is at least one pay period, typically 30 days, and a 13th-month salary is not required by law, so ask whether the contract includes a bonus. The minimum wage is THB 337 to 400 a day, depending on the province.
atlas-th.0073: Whether a graduate can negotiate pay, and how long an employer gives to decide, was not established.
atlas-th.0074: The sponsor must be a registered Thai company with THB 2 million of paid-up capital and four Thai full-time employees for each foreigner, unless it is promoted by the Board of Investment; the employer files the work permit after you enter on a Non-Immigrant B visa.
atlas-th.0075: The employer must show the role cannot easily be filled by a Thai national, and some work is closed to foreigners whatever the permit: 39 occupations, among them accounting and auditing services and Thai law.
atlas-th.0076: Because the employer must show the role cannot easily be filled by a Thai national, tell it early what Thai staff cannot offer: your language, your market or your specialist skill.
atlas-th.0077: JobThai (jobthai.com) and JobsDB (th.jobsdb.com) are the large boards; JobThai has filters for new graduates and internships.
atlas-th.0078: Programme pages: Central Group (careers.centralgroup.com), Deloitte Thailand’s Amplify internships, KBank’s scholarship page and SCB’s careers site. SCG, PTT and the other Big Four sites could not be opened.
atlas-th.0079: University co-operative education offices place students with employers, and fairs such as the WakuWaku Job Fair take walk-ins.
atlas-th.0080: Arriving on a tourist entry to interview and work: from 15 September 2026 visa-free entry for EU citizens is for tourism only, and starting work on a Non-B visa before the work permit is issued is a criminal offence.
atlas-th.0081: Sending an Italian degree with only an Apostille before 28 February 2027, when Thailand still requires full consular legalisation.
atlas-th.0082: Skipping the co-op or internship: it is how employers judge students before hiring, and graduates say their English, digital and soft skills are the gaps.
atlas-th.0083: Aiming at a reserved occupation such as audit sign-off or Thai law: a work permit does not open it.
atlas-th.0084: Employers in the Eastern Economic Corridor expect new hires to communicate in English first and learn technical English later; staff there mostly tested at A2 to B2. Hiring firms test English at recruitment (80% in the ETS survey), usually with the TOEIC.
atlas-th.0085: IT graduates are asked for English at multinationals and Bangkok’s tech firms, and employers name English as one of the four skill gaps of new graduates.
atlas-th.0086: Audit and accountancy services are reserved for Thai nationals, so the work is done in Thai with Thai-licensed professionals; the ACCA qualification is recognised alongside the Thai CPA.
atlas-th.0087: A 2019 YouGov survey of 1,233 Thai graduates found that 52% worked in jobs unrelated to their degree, against 34% of those who had studied abroad; humanities graduates were the most affected, at 67%.
atlas-th.0089: For degree students at universities accredited by the higher-education ministry, applied for on thaievisa.go.th: no re-entry permit needed, extensions handled by the university. No work during studies.
atlas-th.0091: A required, credit-bearing internship uses a Non-Immigrant ED visa with your university’s letter; a paid one also needs a work permit. Any other internship is work in law and needs a Non-B visa and work permit from a qualifying employer. An internship as a tourist leads to arrest.
atlas-th.0093: ED Plus graduates of Thai universities get a one-year extension to look for work, and can switch to a work visa and permit without leaving.
atlas-th.0095: The employer gets a pre-approval letter, you apply for a 90-day Non-B visa, collect the digital work permit, then extend for a year. Ordinary companies need 2 million THB of paid-up capital and four Thai staff per foreigner; BOI-promoted firms are exempt. 40 occupations are closed to foreigners.
atlas-th.0096: SMART and Long-Term Resident visas need no separate work permit, and the LTR offers a 17% flat tax on Thai employment income.
atlas-th.0101: A five-year multiple-entry visa for remote workers with foreign employers or clients: 180 days per entry, extendable once by 180. Working for Thai employers or clients is forbidden.
atlas-th.0104: Thesis research uses a Non-Immigrant ED visa with an agreement between universities; structured research a Non-Immigrant RS visa, only after approval by the National Research Council. Field research without it means losing the visa.
atlas-th.0105: PhD students hold ED Plus; scholarships need no work permit, but paid teaching does.
atlas-th.0106: Thailand has working-holiday agreements only with Australia and New Zealand.
atlas-th.0107: Since 15 September 2026 citizens of 60 countries, the whole EU included, stay up to 30 days visa-free for tourism only, extendable once by 30 days. Fill in the Thailand Digital Arrival Card within three days before arriving; ignore paid “ETA” sites.
